summary: Discovery focused on latency & throughput requirements for EdenPay's payment fraud detection and real-time routing use-cases. Discussed p95 latency targets for streaming vs non-streaming, concurrency profiles, token/sec benchmarking, hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) tradeoffs, KV cache / batching, and security/compliance needs (SOC2, KMS). Agreed next steps: benchmark plan, pricing, and data samples for a pilot.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs
security: SOC2, KMS, VPC, audit logs
benchmark plan and pilot next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samir with Redwood, with me is Laura, our SE. Um, can we do quick intros?
[00:07] Maya: Hi, Maya Thompson, Head of Platform at EdenPay.
[00:10] Diego: Diego Alvarez, SRE.
[00:12] Priya: Priya Nair, VP Eng.
[00:14] Laura: great, thanks. Quick agenda: latency targets, concurrency, streaming behavior, and then security. Sound good?
[00:20] Maya: Yep that works. Our main ask — low p95 for fraud scoring in the payment path, we need to keep p95 under 200ms ideally, and sub-100ms for some high-value flows.
[00:32] Samir: Got it. Are those end-to-end numbers or just model decode?
[00:36] Maya: End-to-end, from request hitting our edge to decision back to the gateway. Network is included.
[00:42] Laura: okay makes sense. Can you share typical payload sizes and token counts?
[00:47] Diego: Usually ~120-250 tokens for the full context, some streams are as short as 30 tokens. We do streaming for live scoring sometimes — like progressive scoring — so we need streaming support and early partial outputs.
[00:58] Samir: When you say streaming, do you need SSE/websocket streams with partial token flushes?
[01:03] Diego: Websocket, yes. We want partials so we can update risk UI before the final decision. p95 for streaming should be as low as possible, realistically under 250ms for first chunk and final under 400ms? But that's fuzzy.
[01:18] Priya: To add, concurrency wise, normal traffic is about 150 concurrent requests during peak, but we have bursts up to 800–1,000 during promotions. We care about graceful degradation — if capacity is constrained we want fallback to a smaller model, or queued fast path.
[01:35] Laura: That's helpful. So two SLOs: p95 end-to-end targets (100ms for critical flows, 200ms for most), and concurrency up to 1k with burst handling. Have you benchmarked token/sec behavior today?
[01:48] Maya: We ran a DIY bench on CloudVendorX endpoints — around 350 tokens/sec on 8x8 GPU endpoints for the primary model. But p95 numbers were variable.
[01:57] Samir: Understood. For Redwood hosted, our multi-tenant offering has predictable latency but with some noisy neighbors; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and predictable p95s — usually lower tail latency. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full isolation but you manage infra.
[02:12] Diego: What's the difference in p95 you'd expect between hosted and dedicated?
[02:16] Laura: Roughly 1.5x–2x better in Dedicated for tail latency in our experience for similar hardware. For example, a model that sees 300ms p95 hosted might be 160–200ms p95 in dedicated with proper batch tuning and KV cache.
[02:30] Maya: When you say KV cache, are you talking about prefix cache of recent prompts? We rely a lot on context reuse for sessionized scoring.
[02:37] Laura: Yes KV cache for autoregressive models — reduces repeated attention compute for overlapping prefixes, improves tokens/sec and tail latency. Also auto-prefix caching at the routing layer helps.
[02:45] Diego: Any mention of quantization here? We are okay with slight quality tradeoff if it halves cost but need to verify false positive rate doesn't change.
[02:54] Samir: We can run quantization profiles per model; Redwood Optimize suggests quantization where acceptable and flags quality regressions tied to your evals.
[03:02] Priya: For the benchmarks, we want token/sec and end-to-end p95, but also a concurrency matrix: 50, 150, 300, 600, 1k. Can Redwood provide a harness?
[03:11] Laura: Yes — I can share our benchmark harness which drives token-level throughput and simulates streaming. We'll need sample payloads and your network topology for e2e numbers.
[03:19] Samir: Also, do you have any regional constraints? We run payments globally but initial pilot will be US region.
[03:25] Maya: US first. Data residency may matter later for EU.
[03:28] Diego: Security items — SOC2 type II, SSO (SAML/Okta), KMS for customer-managed keys, and audit logs tied to requests. Will Redwood hosted support CMK?
[03:37] Laura: On hosted we support envelope encryption with KMS integration; dedicated can support customer-managed KMS; private obviously gives you direct KMS control. We also provide audit logs per-request and token-level cost/latency breakdowns in the Console.
[03:49] Priya: We also need to ensure logs don't contain PII and retention policies are configurable.
[03:54] Samir: Absolutely — retention and redaction options are available, we can share our security pack.
[04:00] Maya: Back to latency: network from our edge to Redwood hosted region adds about 20–30ms. Any suggestions to keep end-to-end low?
[04:06] Laura: You can front with a regional edge or colocate a lightweight proxy; also keep prompt sizes small, use prefix caching, and enable streaming to send partials early. For concurrency, tuning batching windows is key — smaller batch windows reduce tail but increase GPU inefficiency.
[04:23] Diego: For our budget we need price per 1M tokens and also reserved capacity pricing for dedicated. Can you send both?
[04:29] Samir: Yes — we'll send hosted and dedicated quotes plus pilot discounts.
[04:32] Maya: Do you provide SLA numbers for p95?
[04:35] Laura: For Dedicated we can provide latency-based SLAs and uptime SLAs; hosted has uptime SLAs and best-effort latency targets. We'll include specifics in the pricing package.
[04:45] Priya: One more — model fallbacks. Can Redwood route to a smaller/quantized model automatically if the primary is overloaded?
[04:51] Samir: Yes, using smart routing and automated fallback policies. You can define cost or latency based routing and a prioritized list of model variants.
[04:58] Diego: For the benchmark harness, we want three tests: baseline single-request p95, streaming-first-chunk latency, and sustained tokens/sec at concurrency levels.
[05:06] Laura: That's reasonable. We'll capture first-byte and last-byte latencies, tokens/sec, and p95 tails. Also measure GPU utilization for dedicated runs.
[05:14] Maya: Sound good. Any gotchas with websocket streaming and auth tokens?
[05:19] Samir: We support bearer tokens for websocket auth; just ensure idle timeouts on your side match ours if you keep connections warm.
[05:26] Priya: Regarding metrics, we need per-route dashboards, traces, and per-token cost breakdowns for finance.
[05:32] Laura: Console exposes per-route latency, token counts, tail percentiles, and chargebacks. We'll show a demo if helpful after the benchmark.
[05:40] Diego: In your benchmark we'd like to test both with and without KV cache to see delta in p95.
[05:45] Laura: We'll include that. Typically KV cache reduces p95 by 20–40% depending on reuse.
[05:52] Maya: On data privacy, if we go dedicated or private, logs should stay in our VPC and you should only ship aggregated metrics.
[05:59] Samir: Correct. Dedicated provides data isolation. Private puts the control plane in your VPC. We can walk through the architecture.
[06:07] Priya: Okay next, timeline — we'd like a pilot in 2–3 weeks. Is that feasible?
[06:11] Samir: Yes, if we get your traffic sample and a signed pilot order we can provision dedicated pilot capacity in about 7–10 business days. For hosted pilot it's immediate with quotas.
[06:20] Diego: Cost sensitivity — if dedicated is too expensive, can we run hybrid: hosted for non-critical and dedicated for high-critical flows?
[06:26] Laura: Absolutely, hybrid routing is common — route high-priority requests to dedicated, lower-priority to hosted; Redwood's routing can do that by policy.
[06:33] Maya: Competitors we've looked at had struggles with tail latency during bursts. Curious about Redwood's auto-scaling and burst policies.
[06:40] Samir: Dedicated supports autoscale and burst pools; there's also warm pools to reduce cold start tail. We'll propose autoscale config options in the SOW.
[06:49] Priya: For acceptance criteria of the pilot: 200ms p95 for critical flows at 150 concurrency, and 400ms p95 for burst profile at 1k concurrency. Also no regression in fraud detection precision/recall beyond 1%.
[07:03] Samir: Noted — we'll make that part of the benchmark acceptance.
[07:06] Laura: I'll draft a test plan with exact queries and scoring thresholds, and we'll run A/B comparisons across models.
[07:13] Diego: One more operational question: how do you handle KV cache warm-up across replicas?
[07:18] Laura: The runtime shares a prefix cache per model slot and has policies for pre-warming common prefixes. For dedicated we can tune cache TTLs and pre-warm based on historical sessions.
[07:27] Maya: Regarding quantization — we'll need to run a small eval set to ensure FP16->int8 doesn't change scoring.
[07:33] Samir: Redwood Optimize hooks into your eval sets and sends regression alerts if quality drops. We'll include that in the plan.
[07:39] Priya: Ok, anything else on compliance?
[07:42] Diego: We need SOC2 docs and ISO if possible.
[07:45] Laura: We'll send SOC2 report and a security pack after the call.
[07:49] Samir: To recap: Laura shares benchmark harness and plan, Samir sends pricing and pilot SOW, Diego shares traffic samples, and we schedule a dedicated sizing call.
[07:58] Maya: Sounds good.
[08:00] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with artifacts.
[08:04] Priya: Thanks all.
[08:06] [End of recording]
